high-fat and high-carbohydrate rodent diets produce insulin resistance, but different diets produce different effects on insulin action.
different high-fat, high-calorie diets produce different effects on insulin action in rodents.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
high-calorie diets that contain more than 45-50% of total dietary energy from fat or simple carbohydrates reduce insulin action in rodents.
high-calorie diets with more than 45-55% of total energy from fat and/or simple carbohydrates produce insulin resistance.
the more energy a diet contains, the more likely it is to produce insulin resistance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dietary model used is an important factor to consider when interpreting data on insulin action in response to different high-fat diets.
a "high fat diet" is not a "high fat" diet.
the dietary composition and the method used for assessing insulin action are both important factors in determining the effects of high-calorie diets on insulin action.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of high-fat and high-sugar diets on insulin resistance vary widely depending on the type and composition of the diet and the methods used to assess insulin action.
the composition and total macronutrients of the high-fat diet are critical for the development of insulin resistance in the rodent model.

different high-fat and high-carbohydrate diets do not produce identical changes in insulin action, and that the composition of high-calorie diets needs to be considered when interpreting the effects of diet on insulin action.
